meta.title: Icelandic C1 Advanced
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Icelandic → English (see the Icelandic, recall the meaning) and English → Icelandic (see an English meaning, recall the Icelandic). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words of Icelandic for an advanced learner, aligned to C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, and recognise implicit meaning' — a learner here is able to express themselves fluently and spontaneously without much obvious searching for expressions, to use language flexibly and effectively for social, academic and professional purposes, and to produce clear, well-structured, detailed text on complex subjects. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no graded word list for Icelandic as a foreign language was found published, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 63 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — academic and intellectual life, society and governance, the economy and business, law and ethics, mind and behaviour, language and rhetoric, the abstract nouns of analysis, the verbs and adjectives of formal argument, and formal connectors — and the other 1437 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Icelandic, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Icelandic has no word for 'a', so the 1004 nouns carry their gender beside their meaning — masculine, feminine or neuter, which decides every ending the noun and its adjective take — and show the forms a dictionary gives a noun by: the definite (the article is an ending: hesturinn, 'the horse'), the genitive singular and the plural (hests, hestar); behind the All forms fold are its four cases, nominative, accusative, dative and genitive, in both numbers. The 227 verbs show their present 'he' form, past and supine (fer, fór, farið — the forms an Icelandic verb is learnt by), and behind the fold the present in all six persons, the past plural, the past participle and the imperative. Adjectives show their three genders and their comparison. Real example sentences come with 415 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 115 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and the forms of nouns, adjectives and pronouns, and the past and supine of verbs: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). The present tense and imperative of verbs: The Database of Icelandic Morphology (Beygingarlýsing íslensks nútímamáls). The Árni Magnússon Institute for Icelandic Studies. Author and editor Kristín Bjarnadóttir. https://bin.arnastofnun.is (CC BY-SA 4.0) — six present forms and the imperative are taken for each verb, unchanged; nothing else is used. Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0), whose mis-encoded letters (đ for ð, ū for þ) were mapped back before counting. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
